5720: Feeling extremely happy, energized, and alive — as if your whole body and mind have been suddenly "switched on" to full power.
What does it actually feel like?

When someone is exhilarated, they feel a rush of joy and energy at the same time. It's not calm happiness — it's the kind of happiness that makes your heart beat faster, puts a big smile on your face, and makes you feel like you could do anything. There's a sense of being thrilled and refreshed all at once.

Think of the feeling after a roller coaster ride, or the moment you score the winning goal, or when you're running fast with wind in your face. That electric, buzzing, "I feel so alive!" feeling — that's being exhilarated.

Exhilarated sits at the intense end of the happiness scale. It's much stronger than just "happy" or "pleased." It's even stronger than "excited" — because exhilarated also carries a strong sense of energy, vitality, and a kind of refreshed aliveness that excited doesn't always have.

Think of it this way:

  • Happy → you're smiling
  • Excited → your heart is beating faster
  • Exhilarated → your heart is racing, you feel fully alive, energized, and joyful all together
What kinds of things make people feel exhilarated?

Exhilarated is almost always caused by something stimulating, intense, or thrilling — something that engages your full attention and energy:

  • Physical experiences: skiing down a mountain, surfing a big wave, skydiving, running a race
  • Emotional highs: winning a competition, achieving a long-worked-for goal, falling in love
  • Creative moments: finishing a piece of music you composed, giving a speech that moved the crowd
  • Nature and beauty: standing at the top of a mountain and breathing the fresh air, watching a fierce storm safely from indoors
Important nuance: it's not just happiness — it's also energizing

This is what makes "exhilarated" unique. Many words describe happiness, but exhilarated specifically means happiness that charges you up. It makes you feel more awake, more alive, more capable — not sleepy or calm. If someone says they feel exhilarated, you immediately know they have energy and a glow about them.
How is it used in sentences?

• She felt exhilarated after finishing her first marathon.
  • He was completely exhilarated by the thundering sound of the waterfall.
  • The climbers reached the summit and stood there, silent and exhilarated, staring at the world below.
  • I felt exhilarated when the crowd cheered for my performance.
  • Even after hours of hiking in the cold, they were exhilarated, not tired.

Notice how in every sentence, it's not just that someone is happy — they have a charged, full-of-life quality.
Common words and phrases it appears with

• "felt exhilarated"
  • "left me exhilarated"
  • "completely / utterly exhilarated"
  • "exhilarated by the experience / the ride / the challenge"
  • "exhilarated and exhausted" ← very common pairing, because intense physical or emotional experiences often cause both
How it differs from similar words

WordWhat it emphasizes
HappyGeneral positive feeling, calm or mild
ExcitedAnticipation, eagerness — often before something
ThrilledVery pleased and delighted, often about good news
ElatedExtremely happy, often about an achievement — more purely emotional, less physical energy
ExhilaratedA rush of joy plus energy and aliveness — often during or after an intense experience

In plain words: elated is what you feel when you hear wonderful news; exhilarated is what you feel when your body and mind are both buzzing with the joy of an intense, energizing experience.
One-line summary to remember it forever
Exhilarated = so happy and energized that you feel completely, electrically alive.
5721:
When something is exhilarating, it makes you feel intensely alive, joyful, and full of energy — all at the same time, and usually very suddenly. It is the feeling of your heart lifting, your body buzzing with excitement, and your mind feeling wide awake and fully present. It is not quiet happiness. It is a rush.

Think of the moment a rollercoaster drops, or the first breath of cold mountain air, or the final sprint to the finish line of a race you've been training for. That sharp, electric surge of joy and energy — that is what something "exhilarating" produces in you.
The Feeling It Describes — In Depth

"Exhilarating" describes a feeling that has three things happening together:

1. Intense joy — you feel deeply, almost overwhelmingly happy in that moment.

2. A surge of energy — your body feels activated. Your heart might beat faster. You feel awake, powerful, and sharp. This is not the calm joy of sitting by a warm fire. It is the active, charged joy of being in motion or in the middle of something big.

3. A sense of being fully alive — people often describe exhilarating moments as moments when everything else falls away and you are completely in the present, feeling more real and more alive than usual.

All three of these happen together. That combination is what separates "exhilarating" from simpler words like "nice," "exciting," or even "thrilling."

Very strong. "Exhilarating" sits near the top of the scale of positive emotional intensity. It is not a word you use for something mildly pleasant. You would not say "That cup of tea was exhilarating." That would sound strange, almost comical, because the word carries too much force for something quiet and gentle.

It signals a peak experience — a moment that stands out, that moves you, that you remember.
What Kinds of Things Are Called "Exhilarating"?

Almost anything can be described as exhilarating, as long as it produces that charged, alive, energised feeling. Here are the most common categories:

Physical activities and speed:
Skydiving, surfing a big wave, riding a fast motorcycle, skiing down a steep slope — anything involving speed, height, or physical challenge tends to be exhilarating because your body is stimulated and your senses are on full alert.

Nature and the environment:
A strong wind on a cliff top, diving into cold water, standing at the edge of a vast canyon, running through a rainstorm — nature can be exhilarating because it overwhelms your senses in a positive, electric way.

Achievements and moments of success:
Finishing a marathon, delivering a speech you were terrified to give, landing your first job, hearing an audience applaud — these moments are exhilarating because the surge of joy and relief and pride hits all at once.

Art, music, and performance:
A piece of music can be exhilarating if it builds and surges and fills you with energy. A dance performance, a film climax, a live concert — anything that grabs your emotions and accelerates them can be called exhilarating.

Ideas and conversations:
Even a challenging intellectual debate, a sudden brilliant idea, or a conversation that opens your mind completely can be described as exhilarating. The feeling of your thinking expanding rapidly — that energy applies too.

Understanding what a word is not sharpens your understanding of what it is.

Exhilarating ≠ Relaxing. Relaxing is calm and still. Exhilarating is active and charged. They are opposites in energy.

Exhilarating ≠ Merely exciting. "Exciting" is a broader, softer word. Waiting to open a birthday present is exciting. Jumping out of a plane is exhilarating. Exhilarating implies a much greater intensity.

Exhilarating ≠ Happy. You can be quietly, gently happy. Exhilarating happiness is never quiet. It surges.

Exhilarating ≠ Scary (but it can overlap). Some things are both terrifying and exhilarating at the same time — like bungee jumping. This is actually very common. The two feelings can co-exist, and people often describe this mix as part of what makes something exhilarating.

"Exhilarating" almost always has a positive meaning, but the experience itself might involve discomfort, fear, or difficulty. A freezing cold swim is physically uncomfortable, yet people often describe it as exhilarating. A gruelling mountain climb is exhausting, yet the experience can be exhilarating.

The key is that even when the activity is hard or scary, the overall feeling it produces is positive, energising, and life-affirming. The difficulty becomes part of what makes it feel so electric.

Here are several sentences showing how "exhilarating" works in real contexts. Notice how the word always signals that rush of aliveness and energy.

  • "The first time she rode a horse at full gallop, the experience was completely exhilarating — she felt like she was flying."
  • "Standing at the top of the mountain after a six-hour climb, the wind in his face and the whole world spread below him, was one of the most exhilarating moments of his life."
  • "There is something exhilarating about starting a completely new chapter — a new city, a new job, a blank page."
  • "The crowd's roar when he scored the winning goal was exhilarating beyond anything he had ever felt."
  • "She found the debate surprisingly exhilarating — her mind was racing, her arguments were sharp, and she felt completely alive."
  • "Even after years of performing, the actor still found walking onto a live stage exhilarating."
How to Use This Word Correctly

Use it for experiences, not objects. You would not normally call a chair or a book "exhilarating" unless you mean it produced that feeling in you. You say "the ride was exhilarating" or "it was an exhilarating experience" — not "what an exhilarating table."

Use it for intensity. Save this word for moments that genuinely produce a strong rush. Using it for small, everyday pleasures will make your language feel exaggerated.

Pair it with experiences of aliveness. Speed, freedom, achievement, nature, performance, discovery — these are the natural homes of this word.

If you had to reduce this entire word to one sentence:

Something exhilarating makes you feel intensely, electrically alive — a powerful rush of joy and energy that fills your whole body and mind at once.

That is the heart of it. Every use of the word, in every sentence you will ever encounter it, will come back to that feeling.
5722:
Exhilaration is a powerful, electric feeling of intense joy, excitement, and energy that surges through you during or after something thrilling, freeing, or deeply stimulating. It is not just feeling good — it is a feeling that wakes every part of you up, floods you with vitality, and makes you feel completely, brilliantly alive.

Think of standing at the top of a mountain after a long climb, or the moment a roller coaster begins its first drop. Your heart pounds, your senses sharpen, your whole body feels charged. That overwhelming rush of aliveness is exhilaration.
What Makes It Different from Simple Happiness

This is important, because exhilaration is often confused with just "being happy" — but they are not the same.

Happiness is warm, calm, and steady. You can feel happy sitting quietly with a good book.

Exhilaration is sharp, electric, and energetic. It sweeps through you like a wave. It has a physical quality — a racing heart, a sense of breathlessness, a feeling of being lit from the inside. You cannot feel exhilarated while sitting still and calm. It always comes with a charge of energy.

A simple way to remember it: happiness can be quiet; exhilaration is always loud, even if only on the inside.

Because this word describes something that is both emotional and physical, it helps to picture what it actually feels like in the body:

  • Your heart beats faster than usual.
  • You feel wide awake and alert, not tired.
  • You may feel slightly breathless, as if the moment has taken your breath away.
  • There is a tingling, buzzing sensation — sometimes called a "rush."
  • You feel energized, not drained — even if you have just done something exhausting.

This physical quality is one of exhilaration's defining features. It is not a soft or gentle emotion. It crackles.

Exhilaration is typically triggered by things that are thrilling, stimulating, freeing, or tied to a great achievement. Common triggers include:

  • Physical adventure — skydiving, skiing down a steep slope, surfing a big wave, swimming in cold open water.
  • Achievement after great effort — crossing a finish line, finishing a difficult exam, completing something you worked hard for.
  • Sudden wonderful news — being told you got the job, the scholarship, the role you wanted.
  • Vast, awe-inspiring nature — standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon, watching a storm roll in over the ocean.
  • Creative or artistic peak moments — a musician hitting the perfect note in front of a roaring crowd, an actor walking off a stage after a perfect performance.

Notice that all of these involve intensity — either of sensation, effort, beauty, or surprise. Exhilaration does not come from ordinary, everyday moments. It comes when something pushes you beyond the usual.

Exhilaration sits at the high end of positive emotions. It is stronger than pleasure, deeper than amusement, and more energetic than contentment. It is a peak feeling — the kind you remember vividly long after the moment has passed.

It is also temporary by nature. It rises sharply and then fades. You cannot stay exhilarated for hours on end. What lingers afterward is often a warm glow of happiness, but the exhilaration itself — that sharp, electric charge — belongs to the moment.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Excitement is close to exhilaration, but weaker and more forward-looking. You feel excited before something happens (a concert you're about to attend). Exhilaration is more likely to hit you during or right after the peak moment itself. Exhilaration is also more intense — excitement is a simmer; exhilaration is a boil.

Euphoria is also intense, but it has a dreamy, floaty quality — almost unreal, like you are floating above the world. Exhilaration is sharper and more grounded. It keeps you in the moment, fiercely present.

Thrill refers more to the exciting event or stimulus itself ("What a thrill!"), while exhilaration is the feeling that the thrill produces inside you.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

The word flows naturally in both formal writing and everyday speech, though it leans slightly literary:

  • "She felt a wave of exhilaration as the plane lifted off the runway for the first time in her life."
  • "There was a pure, clean exhilaration in running through the rain."
  • "The exhilaration of reaching the summit was unlike anything he had ever experienced."
  • "After delivering the speech she had feared for weeks, an unexpected exhilaration came over her."

You will also see it used in modified forms to add shade to the meaning:

  • Sheer exhilaration — pure, absolute, uncut exhilaration.
  • A rush of exhilaration — emphasizes how quickly and powerfully the feeling arrives.
  • The exhilaration of [something] — links the feeling to its specific cause.

If you ever need to recall this word in an instant: exhilaration is the intense, electric feeling of joy and aliveness that rushes through you when something thrilling or wonderful happens — more physical and more powerful than ordinary happiness, always energizing, and impossible to fake.
5723:
To exhort someone means to strongly and earnestly urge them to do something, usually because you genuinely believe it is important, right, or necessary. It sits in a specific zone of human communication — stronger than a casual suggestion, but not quite an order. Think of it as passionate, heartfelt encouragement with real moral weight behind it.

When you exhort someone, you are essentially saying: "I deeply care about this, I believe in you, and I am urging you — with everything I have — to do this."
Breaking Down What Makes It Special

Three things set "exhort" apart from ordinary words like "ask" or "tell":

1. It carries emotional and moral sincerity. The person doing the exhorting is not being casual. They genuinely feel that what they are urging matters — morally, personally, or urgently. A coach who exhorts his team to fight until the final whistle is not simply giving instructions. He is pouring conviction into his words.

2. It is a strong push, not a command. If you order someone, they must obey — you have authority over them. If you exhort someone, you have no such power. You are appealing to their will, their conscience, their spirit. The other person still has the freedom to say no. This is why exhortation is often used by leaders, teachers, coaches, and speakers — people who lead through inspiration rather than force.

3. It is sustained and purposeful. You don't exhort someone in a single throwaway sentence. It implies deliberate, focused effort to move someone toward action. There is a sense of leaning in — of really pressing the point home.

The most common pattern is straightforward:

Exhort + someone + to + do something

  • The general exhorted his soldiers to hold the line.
  • She exhorted her students to keep practicing even when it felt hopeless.
  • The coach exhorted the team to give everything in the final minutes.
  • He exhorted the crowd to stay calm and trust the process.

Notice that each sentence involves someone urging another person (or group) toward a specific action, with an underlying sense of urgency and genuine care.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where the word really comes into focus. English has many words for urging people, and understanding where "exhort" sits among them is the key to truly owning it.

Ask is plain and neutral. "I asked him to help" has no emotional weight at all. Exhort is far more intense.

Suggest is even lighter — it is barely a nudge. Exhort is the opposite of a nudge.

Advise is professional and measured, like a doctor telling you what to do for your health. Exhort is warmer, more passionate, and less clinical.

Encourage is positive but gentle. If you encourage someone, you are supporting them softly. If you exhort them, you are pushing them with urgency and fire.

Urge is the closest common synonym — and in most situations you can use the two interchangeably. But "exhort" feels slightly more formal, more sustained, and often implies a public or moral dimension. A politician urges you to vote; a prophet exhorts you to repent. Both push, but exhort pushes with deeper earnestness.

Implore / Beseech / Plead involve desperation and often a sense of vulnerability — like you are at someone's mercy. Exhort does not feel desperate. It feels powerful and convinced, not helpless.

Order / Command involve authority — the other person has little choice. Exhort carries no such authority. It works through inspiration, not hierarchy.

Preach is close in spirit, but it often carries a negative tone — like someone is being self-righteous or talking down to you. Exhort is free from that baggage. It is earnest without being preachy.

Exhort is a formal word. You will encounter it in speeches, literature, religious texts, historical writing, journalism, and formal essays. You are unlikely to hear someone say in casual conversation: "Hey, I just want to exhort you to try that new café." That would sound stiff and odd.

In natural speech, people tend to say "urge," "push," or "tell." But when writing formally, or when you want to convey the full emotional and moral weight of an appeal, "exhort" is the right word.

Imagine a great leader standing before a tired, discouraged army. They have come a long way and have little left in them. The leader steps forward and speaks with absolute conviction — not giving an order, not making a polite suggestion, but calling on every ounce of courage and will in each person. That is exhortation. It lives in that space where language becomes an act of moral persuasion, where the speaker is trying not just to inform the listener, but to move them.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To exhort is to strongly urge someone to take action, with genuine passion, conviction, and moral seriousness — without commanding them or ordering them. It is what a great coach, leader, teacher, or speaker does when they are not just talking at someone, but are reaching into them and pulling out their best.
5724: An exhortation is a strong, sincere, and earnest urging — spoken or written — that tries to move someone to take action, behave in a certain way, or sometimes to stop doing something harmful. It is more than casual advice. It carries emotional weight, urgency, and genuine conviction. The person giving an exhortation truly believes the matter is important — sometimes even critical — and wants the other person to feel that importance deeply enough to act on it.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

This is where most learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Exhortation vs. Advice: Advice is calm, neutral, and informational. An exhortation is charged with urgency and feeling. A doctor telling you what foods to eat is advice. That same doctor leaning forward, looking you in the eye, and earnestly urging you to change your lifestyle before your heart gives out — that is an exhortation.

Exhortation vs. Encouragement: Encouragement says "You can do it." An exhortation says "You must do it — and here is why it truly matters." Encouragement lifts your confidence. An exhortation stirs your conscience and will.

Exhortation vs. a Command or Order: A command demands obedience and can enforce compliance. An exhortation appeals to your heart, your conscience, or your sense of reason. It urges strongly but does not force. You are still free to refuse — but the person giving the exhortation is making every effort to make sure you don't.

Exhortation vs. a Plea: A plea usually comes from desperation or helplessness — someone begging because they have no power. An exhortation, by contrast, typically comes from a place of authority, care, or moral strength. It is assertive, not desperate.
The Tone and Feel of an Exhortation

Exhortations are almost always serious in tone. They are passionate and purposeful. You would never describe a casual, throwaway remark as an exhortation. The word implies that something significant is at stake — a person's wellbeing, a moral choice, a mission, a cause.

Exhortations can be brief or long. A single powerful sentence can be an exhortation. So can an entire speech. What defines it is not length, but intensity and intent — the sincere desire to move someone toward something meaningful.

You will encounter this word most often in these settings:

Religious contexts — This is perhaps the most traditional home of the word. Sermons, scriptures, and spiritual writings are filled with exhortations. "Love your neighbour," "Seek justice," "Do not be afraid" — these are all exhortations. Many religious texts even have entire sections formally called exhortations.

Political speeches — Leaders use exhortation to rally people behind a cause or a moment in history. Think of a president urging a nation to unite in a time of crisis, or a revolutionary leader calling people to stand up for their freedom.

Sports and coaching — A coach's half-time speech, delivered with fire and conviction to a struggling team, is a classic exhortation. It is not a tactical briefing — it is an attempt to reignite the team's will and spirit.

Literature and formal writing — Characters in novels, plays, and epic poems often deliver exhortations at dramatic turning points. Leaders address their armies. Parents address their children at life's crossroads. Mentors urge their students toward greatness.

Everyday life — While the word itself is formal, the act happens all around us. A parent sitting down with a teenager and earnestly urging them to make better choices is giving an exhortation, even if no one uses that word.
The Register of the Word Itself

The word exhortation is formal and somewhat elevated in register. In casual everyday speech, you would more likely say "pep talk," "urging," or "push." But when you use the word exhortation, you signal that what happened was serious, dignified, and purposeful — not a passing comment, but a deliberate and heartfelt appeal.

These will show you how the word behaves in real use:

  • "The general's exhortation before the battle filled the soldiers with renewed courage."
  • "Despite repeated exhortations from her family and doctors, she refused to rest."
  • "His exhortation to 'always choose honesty, even when it costs you' stayed with me for the rest of my life."
  • "The priest closed the service with a moving exhortation about compassion and forgiveness."
  • "The coach's halftime exhortation turned the game around completely."
  • "She wrote a passionate exhortation to young people, urging them to take climate change seriously."

Since you'll encounter this word family in your reading:

Exhort is the verb form. "She exhorted her students to never give up on their dreams." To exhort someone means to give them an exhortation.

Exhortatory or exhortative are the adjective forms, meaning something that has the quality of an exhortation. "The letter had a distinctly exhortatory tone." These are less common but worth knowing.

An exhortation is a strong, heartfelt, and earnest urging — delivered from a place of care, conviction, or authority — that tries to move someone to meaningful action, appealing to their will, conscience, or better judgment rather than forcing them to comply.
5725:
Exhumation is the act of digging up a dead body — or other buried remains — that was previously placed underground.

Think of it as the exact opposite of burial. When someone dies, their body is buried (lowered into the ground and covered with soil). Exhumation reverses that process: the body is carefully dug back up and brought to the surface. Simple as that.

Most commonly, a human corpse — but the word can also apply to:

  • Skeletal remains (bones that are all that's left after decomposition)
  • Cremated ashes that were buried in an urn
  • Ancient human remains discovered at a burial site
  • In rare uses, buried objects of significant value or importance
Why Would Anyone Do This? (The Real-World Contexts)

This is where the word gets rich and interesting. Exhumation happens for several very different reasons:

1. Criminal Investigations & Legal Reasons

This is probably the most dramatic context you'll encounter the word in. If there is suspicion that a person was murdered, poisoned, or did not die the way originally reported, a court or law enforcement authority can legally order an exhumation. The body is then re-examined by forensic experts — scientists who study bodies to uncover the truth about how a person died.

For example, if someone was buried 10 years ago and new evidence suggests they were poisoned, a judge might order an exhumation so that the body can be tested for poison. The results can be used in a criminal trial.

2. To Correct or Confirm Cause of Death

Sometimes the original doctor who examined the body made a mistake, or didn't have access to modern testing methods. An exhumation allows medical professionals to take a second, more thorough look — using updated science — to determine the true cause of death.

3. Moving or Relocating Remains

Families sometimes want their loved one reburied in a different place — perhaps closer to other family members, or in a homeland the person was connected to. This requires an exhumation. Similarly, when a cemetery must be cleared to make way for construction or development, the bodies are exhumed and moved to a new burial site.

4. Religious & Cultural Practices

In certain cultures and religious traditions, exhumation is not unusual — it is actually a planned part of the burial process. For example, in some Greek Orthodox communities, it is traditional to exhume the bones of the deceased a few years after burial, clean them, and place them in a special storage place called an ossuary. This is considered a respectful and sacred practice.

5. Archaeological & Historical Research

When scientists or historians dig up ancient burial grounds to study past civilizations, the uncovering of human remains can be described as an exhumation. For example, examining the remains of an Egyptian pharaoh or a medieval peasant to understand how people lived (and died) long ago.

BurialPlacing a body into the ground
ExhumationTaking a buried body back out of the ground

They are direct opposites of each other. If you remember nothing else, remember this: burial goes in, exhumation comes out.

Here's how you'll typically see it used:

  • "The family was devastated when the court ordered the exhumation of their mother's body."
  • "After the exhumation, forensic scientists discovered traces of arsenic in the bones."
  • "The exhumation of the ancient warrior's remains revealed a surprisingly advanced form of surgery had been performed on his skull."
  • "The cemetery's exhumation was carried out carefully to ensure every set of remains was treated with dignity before being moved."

Language is creative, and "exhumation" is sometimes used metaphorically — meaning it's used to describe bringing something long-buried or long-forgotten back into the open, even when no actual body or grave is involved.

For example:

  • "The journalist's investigation was an exhumation of decades-old government secrets."
  • "The film felt like an exhumation of a musical era everyone had forgotten."

In these cases, the speaker is painting a vivid picture: just as a literal exhumation brings something buried back to the surface, a figurative exhumation brings hidden truths, memories, or forgotten things back into the light. This usage is literary and somewhat poetic — you'll find it more in writing than in everyday speech.

• Exhume (verb) — the action: "They decided to exhume the body."
  • Exhumed (past tense verb / adjective) — "The exhumed remains were sent to a laboratory."
  • Exhumation (noun) — the event or process itself: "The exhumation took place at dawn."
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Exhumation" is a formal, serious word. You won't hear it in casual conversation. It belongs to the language of law, medicine, forensics, archaeology, and journalism. When you see it, it almost always signals that something significant — legal, historical, or deeply personal — is happening. It carries a weight to it, because it involves the dead and the respect owed to them.

It is never a trivial or light word.
5726:
To exhume something means to dig it up from the ground after it has been buried.

That's the heart of it. But there's more texture to this word than that simple definition suggests, so let's go deeper.

In its most direct, physical sense, exhume almost always refers to digging up a dead body that was previously buried — usually in a grave.

When a person dies, their body is typically buried underground as part of a funeral. That burial is meant to be permanent. But sometimes, for important reasons, the body needs to be brought back up to the surface. That act — the deliberate, careful removal of a buried body from the earth — is what it means to exhume.

Think of it this way: burial takes something down into the earth. Exhuming reverses that. It brings what was underground back above ground.

Example: Investigators exhumed the body to find out whether the man had actually been poisoned.
Why Would Someone Exhume a Body?

Understanding why exhumation happens helps you understand the weight of the word. It's not something done casually. Common reasons include:

  • Criminal investigations — If there is new suspicion that a person was murdered, detectives may need to re-examine the remains for evidence (such as signs of poisoning or violence) that wasn't discovered initially.
  • Medical or scientific re-examination — Sometimes a second, more thorough autopsy is needed to establish the true cause of death.
  • Legal proceedings — A court may officially order a body to be exhumed when the circumstances of someone's death become the subject of a legal dispute.
  • Identification purposes — In historical cases, graves of notable people are sometimes opened to confirm the identity of the remains using modern techniques like DNA testing.
  • Relocation — A family may have a loved one's remains exhumed so they can be reburied somewhere else — in a different cemetery, or closer to family.

This tells you something important about the tone of the word: exhume carries a sense of seriousness and gravity. It is not an everyday event. It involves permission, procedure, and usually a compelling reason.

Like many powerful words, exhume is also used figuratively — that is, not literally about digging up bodies, but about bringing something back that was long buried, hidden, forgotten, or suppressed.

The logic is the same: something was put away and out of sight, and now it is being brought back into the open.

Examples:

  • The biographer exhumed forgotten letters that revealed the truth about the poet's private life.
  • Therapy sometimes forces you to exhume painful memories you thought you had buried forever.
  • The new documentary exhumed a scandal that the government had tried hard to keep hidden.

In these uses, the "buried" thing isn't a body — it's information, a memory, a secret, or a piece of history. But the feeling is the same: something deliberately or naturally hidden away is now being pulled back into the light, often uncomfortably.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Exhume is a formal word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. It belongs to the language of:

  • News reporting (especially crime or investigative journalism)
  • Legal and courtroom language
  • Medical and forensic science
  • Serious literary or academic writing

If you said "they dug up the body," that's informal and blunt. If you said "the body was exhumed," it sounds official, clinical, and deliberate. Both describe the same act, but exhume signals that the process was sanctioned, formal, and purposeful — not random digging.
The Key Distinction: What Makes Exhume Different from Just "Dig Up"

You might wonder: why not just say "dig up"? Here's the difference:

  • Dig up is general. You can dig up potatoes, a garden, a pipe, or a treasure chest.
  • Exhume is specific. It refers almost exclusively to retrieving something — especially a body — that was deliberately buried, and doing so with intention and often with authority or official sanction.

Exhume also implies reversal of a prior, intentional act. Something was buried on purpose. Exhuming it is the deliberate undoing of that burial. That sense of reversal and seriousness is baked into the word.
• Exhumation (noun) — The act or process of exhuming. "The court approved the exhumation of the remains." If exhume is the action, exhumation is the name for that event or process.

What it meansTo dig up something — especially a dead body — that was previously buried
FigurativelyTo bring back something long hidden, forgotten, or suppressed
ToneFormal, serious, weighty
Common contextsCriminal investigations, legal cases, forensic science, history, journalism
Key nuanceImplies a deliberate reversal of a prior burial, often done with authority

To put it all in one sentence: to exhume is to deliberately bring something — most often a buried body — back out of the ground, or, figuratively, to surface something that had been long buried in obscurity, silence, or secrecy.

Exigence means an urgent need, demand, or pressing requirement that arises from a specific situation. Think of it as what a situation forces upon you — the unavoidable call to act, respond, or address something because the circumstances make it critical.

It also refers, more broadly, to the pressing situation itself — a state of affairs so urgent or critical that it demands an immediate response.

Imagine you're calmly going about your day. Then something happens — a crisis, a problem, an opportunity that won't wait. That thing, that pressing circumstance which is suddenly pulling at you and demanding your attention and action? That is an exigence.

It's not just any need. It's a need with urgency baked into it. It's the gap between how things are and how they need to be, and it's sharp enough that you cannot ignore it.
The Two Layers of Its Meaning

Layer 1 — The urgent requirement placed on you:
The exigence of a flooded basement is that you must act right now to prevent damage. The situation itself is creating a demand. You didn't choose the demand; the circumstances imposed it.

Layer 2 — The urgent situation itself:
You could say, "She responded calmly to the exigence of the moment." Here, exigence is the crisis or pressing circumstance — the thing you're responding to.

Both layers are really the same coin flipped two ways: the urgent situation and the urgent demand it creates are inseparable.
How It's Used in Everyday Language

"Exigence" tends to appear in formal, serious, or academic writing. You won't often hear it in casual conversation — people usually say "urgency," "pressing need," or "crisis" instead. But when you do encounter "exigence," it signals something specific: not just that something is urgent, but that the situation itself is what's generating that urgency.

Some natural examples:

  • "The exigence of war demanded rapid innovation in medicine." — The war created an urgent, unavoidable need; it wasn't optional.
  • "She was a leader who rose well to every exigence." — Every crisis, every pressing demand that circumstances threw at her.
  • "The exigences of the moment left no room for hesitation." — (plural) The combined urgent demands of the situation.
Important: Its Specific Meaning in Rhetoric and Writing

If you ever study writing, communication, literature, or rhetoric, you will encounter "exigence" used in a very precise, technical way — and it's important to know this.

In rhetoric (the study of how communication works and persuades), exigence means the specific problem, issue, or imperfect condition in the world that calls a piece of writing or speech into existence in the first place.

Every piece of communication — a speech, an essay, a letter, a news article — exists because something prompted it. That something is the exigence.

Think of it this way: before any speech is delivered, something happened. A crisis emerged. An injustice occurred. A question went unanswered. A decision needed to be made. That pressing, real-world condition — the thing that made communicating necessary right now — is the rhetorical exigence.

Examples:

  • Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech: The exigence was the ongoing oppression and denial of civil rights for Black Americans — a deep and urgent wrong that demanded to be addressed publicly, immediately, and powerfully.
  • A doctor publishing a study about a new dangerous drug interaction: The exigence is the danger itself — the gap between what people know and what they urgently need to know to stay safe.
  • A president addressing the nation after a natural disaster: The exigence is the disaster and the public's fear, confusion, and need for leadership.

In this rhetorical sense, exigence answers the question: "Why does this communication exist? What urgent, real-world situation made it necessary?"

A key nuance in the rhetorical meaning: the exigence must be something that can actually be addressed or improved through communication. A fixed, unchangeable fact of nature (like the sun rising every morning) isn't an exigence, because no speech can change it. An exigence is always a condition that human response — through words, action, or both — can actually influence.
How Exigence Differs from Similar Words

• Urgency is a quality or feeling — the sense that something is pressing. Exigence is more concrete: it's the actual situation or demand, not just a feeling about it.
  • Necessity suggests something that must happen, often regardless of context. Exigence is always rooted in a specific situation — it's the circumstances that are doing the demanding.
  • Emergency is a sudden, dangerous situation. Exigence is broader — it doesn't have to be an emergency. It can be a persistent, serious condition or an urgent but non-dangerous need.
  • Requirement is neutral — a rule or condition you must meet. Exigence carries real weight and urgency; it's not just a checkbox but a pressing, live demand.

The word has two accepted plural forms: exigences and exigencies. In practice, exigencies is far more common, especially in speech and formal writing. Both mean the same thing.

"The exigencies of running a country during wartime are immense." — All the urgent, pressing demands and requirements that arise from that situation.
Exigence is the urgent, pressing demand — or the urgent, pressing situation — that makes action or communication not just useful, but genuinely necessary.
5728:
An exigency is an urgent, pressing situation or need that demands immediate attention or action. It is something that cannot wait — the circumstances make it critical that you act now.

Think of it this way: when a situation becomes so demanding and pressing that it forces your hand and leaves you no choice but to respond, that situation — or the urgent need it creates — is an exigency.

This word carries two senses that are deeply connected, and understanding both will give you complete command of it.

Sense 1 — The urgent situation itself. Here, "exigency" refers to a crisis, an emergency, or a critical moment that demands a response. The word points to the situation that is pressing in on you.

"In times of exigency, a leader cannot afford to hesitate."

Here, "exigency" means a time of urgent crisis — a moment when things are critical and pressing.

Sense 2 — The demands or requirements that an urgent situation creates. Here, "exigency" refers not to the situation itself but to the needs and requirements that the situation imposes on you. This sense is almost always used in the plural: exigencies.

"The soldiers had to adapt constantly to the exigencies of war."

Here, "exigencies of war" means the pressing demands, harsh requirements, and urgent necessities that war forces upon people — the things war makes you do or deal with whether you like it or not.
Singular vs. Plural — An Important Distinction

When used in the singular ("an exigency"), the word usually refers to one specific urgent situation or pressing need.

"The doctor cited medical exigency and began operating immediately."

When used in the plural ("exigencies"), it refers to the ongoing, multiple demands and pressures that a difficult circumstance keeps placing on you — the relentless requirements of a hard situation.

"She juggled the exigencies of raising three children while running a business."

Both usages are correct and common. Just know that the plural form is far more frequently seen in practice.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Exigency" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of pressure, urgency, and unavoidability. When you use it, you are communicating that the need in question is not optional or convenient — it is forced upon you by circumstances. There is a weight to it that words like "need" or "requirement" simply don't carry.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Several words are close to "exigency," but each has a slightly different flavor:

Emergency focuses on danger — something sudden and dangerous that needs rescue or intervention. An emergency is usually a one-time event.

Urgency is the quality of being urgent. It describes how pressing something feels, but it doesn't refer to a situation itself.

Necessity means something that is required or unavoidable, but it doesn't necessarily imply time pressure.

Exigency combines the urgency of emergency, the unavoidability of necessity, and the pressure of urgency — all at once. It says: "This situation is pressing, it demands action, and you cannot ignore it." It is the most loaded and forceful of the four.
The Register: Where and When This Word Is Used

"Exigency" is a formal word. You will not hear it in casual everyday conversation. Instead, you will encounter it in formal writing, journalism, legal or official documents, academic texts, military contexts, and serious literature. Knowing this matters, because using it in casual speech would sound oddly stiff — but using it in formal writing signals precision and sophistication.

Here are examples showing how versatile the word is across different settings:

Medical: "The surgeon acted without consent due to medical exigency — the patient would not have survived the delay."

Political/Military: "The general made difficult decisions under the exigencies of battle, choices he never would have made in peacetime."

Business: "The exigencies of the market forced the company to pivot its entire strategy within weeks."

Personal life: "Raising a seriously ill child taught her to respond calmly to any exigency."

Law: "The law allows certain powers to be exercised only in cases of genuine national exigency."

If you ever need to recall this word instantly, remember: exigency = an urgent situation, or the urgent demands that a difficult situation forces upon you. It always involves pressure, unavoidability, and the need to act now.
5729:
Imagine you're in a situation that is so urgent, so pressing, so demanding that it simply cannot wait. It is screaming at you to act — right now. That feeling is the heart of the word exigent.

Exigent means: requiring immediate attention or action, OR making very heavy demands on someone.

It actually carries two closely related meanings, and understanding both will give you the complete picture.
Meaning 1: Urgently Pressing (the most common meaning)

When something is exigent, it is not just important — it is critically urgent. It is a situation where delay would be dangerous, harmful, or simply unacceptable. There is a strong sense of pressure baked into this word.

Think of it as a step beyond "urgent." Something urgent needs attention soon. Something exigent needs attention immediately — it is bearing down on you.

Examples:

  • "The flooding created an exigent situation that forced the rescue teams to abandon their plan and act instantly."
  • "Her exigent need for medical care meant there was no time to wait for paperwork."
  • "The commander responded to the exigent threat without hesitation."

In each case, notice that there is a quality of pressure and no-room-for-delay in the situation being described. The word signals that the stakes are high and time is short.
Meaning 2: Making Very Heavy Demands (on a person)

The second meaning shifts from describing situations to describing people or things that make excessive or very difficult demands. An exigent person is one who expects a great deal — they are hard to satisfy, relentless in their standards, and they push you hard.

Examples:

  • "Her exigent professor expected not just correct answers, but flawlessly reasoned arguments every single time."
  • "Working for such an exigent client was exhausting — nothing was ever good enough."
  • "The role was technically rewarding but exigent in its demands on the team's time and energy."

This meaning shares DNA with Meaning 1: in both cases, something is pressing heavily on you — either a situation pressing you to act immediately, or a person pressing you to perform at a very high level.
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Both meanings share a single underlying quality: pressure that cannot be ignored.

  • A situation that is exigent → presses you to act now.
  • A person who is exigent → presses you to give more.

The word always implies that something heavy is being demanded of you, with little room to negotiate or delay.

Exigent is a formal word. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation. Instead, you'll encounter it in:

  • Legal writing — This is where the word is most famous. The phrase "exigent circumstances" is a widely used legal term, particularly in criminal law. It refers to emergency situations so urgent that normal legal procedures (like getting a warrant before searching someone's home) can be bypassed. For example, if police are chasing a suspect who just entered a house, or if someone inside is in immediate danger, the law may allow them to enter without a warrant because the circumstances are exigent — there is simply no time to follow the usual process.
  • Journalism and formal writing — describing crises, emergencies, or pressing problems.
  • Literature and academic writing — to describe demanding conditions or urgent needs.
  • Professional settings — business, medicine, or government, where formal language is common.
How It Sits Among Similar Words

It helps to see how exigent compares to words with overlapping meanings:

  • Urgent — Something urgent needs attention soon. Something exigent needs it right now, with higher stakes and more pressure. Exigent is the more intense, formal version.
  • Pressing — Very similar to exigent in Meaning 1, but "pressing" is more everyday and slightly softer. "Pressing matter" feels common; "exigent matter" feels weighty and formal.
  • Critical — "Critical" can simply mean very important, even without time pressure. Exigent always implies urgency or demand — not just importance.
  • Demanding — Similar to Meaning 2 of exigent, but "demanding" is casual and widely used. "Exigent" in this sense is its formal, elevated counterpart.

These are the word combinations you're most likely to see:

  • Exigent circumstances — the most common usage, especially in law. Means an emergency situation that justifies bypassing normal rules.
  • Exigent needs — urgent, pressing needs.
  • Exigent situation — a situation demanding immediate action.
  • Exigent demands — very heavy or difficult demands placed on someone.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear exigent, ask yourself: "Is something pressing hard, either on a situation (urgently) or on a person (demandingly)?" If yes — that's exigent.

Think of it as the formal, high-stakes version of saying: "This cannot wait" or "This expects a great deal."

Exigent describes either a situation so urgent it demands immediate action, or a person/thing that makes very heavy and relentless demands — always carrying a strong sense of pressure that cannot be ignored or postponed.
